Cessna 152 and Cessna 340A

Two calls, one runway

Two small planes head for the same runway in Watsonville, California, and both pilots are talking on the radio. 3 people died.

Watsonville, 18 August 2022

Laps on a clear afternoon

A Cessna 152, a small two seat plane, flies laps at Watsonville, landing again and again. Its pilot is not talking to air traffic control. On most legs of his last four laps he calls his position on the shared frequency, the CTAF.

Turlock14:32

A twin leaves Turlock

A twin engine Cessna 340 takes off from Turlock with its pilot and a passenger, bound for runway 20 at Watsonville. Controllers give it flight following and, at the end, warn of other planes in the Watsonville pattern.

Words on this page
flight following a service in which air traffic controllers watch a small airplane on radar during its trip and point out other traffic to the pilot
traffic pattern the standard rectangular loop that airplanes fly around an airport so that takeoffs and landings happen in an orderly flow

How small airports work

The loop and the shortcut

Photo Dan Dawson, public domain

The FAA regulates traffic pattern flow, not how pilots join it. Pilots may come straight in, but should not disrupt the traffic flow. The standard pattern is still encouraged, above all when other traffic is around.

What really happened

Keep coming straight in

He keeps coming straight in and next calls one mile out. Both keep making position calls, but they have not yet talked to each other.

Left base

Looking for each other

The 152 pilot turns onto left base, the leg just before final. About 19 seconds later the 340 pilot calls one mile out, looking for traffic on left base. The 152 pilot answers that he sees the 340, behind him.

On the airport

Three lives lost

All three people die, the 152 pilot and the pilot and passenger of the 340. The 152 comes down on airport land about 1,200 feet short of runway 20. The 340 ends up in a hangar storage room, and a fire breaks out outside the hangar.

Clue 1 of 3

Recorded ADS-B data trace the 340 from Turlock all the way to the collision.

How fast is the 340 on its approach?

{{ o.t }}
{{ verdict }}

About 180 knots ground speed, and the 340 holds it until the collision.

Clue 2 of 3

In the 340 wreckage, the flaps and the landing gear are retracted.

What does that tell you?

{{ o.t }}
{{ verdict }}

This fits a pilot who had not set the airplane up for landing. Neither airplane showed signs of a mechanical fault.

Words on this page
flaps panels at the back of the wing that slide out to let an airplane fly slower for takeoff and landing
retractable landing gear wheels that fold up into the airplane after takeoff to reduce drag and must be lowered again before landing

What witnesses told investigators

Two people watching

The pilot overhead was at 1,300 feet and heard both pilots on the radio getting close. He saw the 340 moving much quicker than usual for landing. Someone on the ground photographed both airplanes before the collision.

The cause

The probable cause

The pilot of the twin engine 340 (the report's "multi-engine airplane"), flying straight in, did not see and avoid the single engine 152.
Also found
  • When flight following ended, controllers told him to use caution for other planes in the pattern.
  • Both pilots made proper position calls but only spoke to each other at about one mile out.
The official wording
Words on this page
see and avoid the basic rule that pilots flying in good weather must keep looking out for other aircraft and steer clear of them
multi-engine having more than one engine, such as a twin engine airplane
Next chapter

In the report's words

“The failure of the pilot of the multi-engine airplane to see and avoid the single-engine airplane while performing a straight-in approach for landing.”

NTSB report WPR22FA309, word for word

The FAA handbook
80 to 90knots

Typical handbook pattern speed for fast retractables. Maker's speeds come first. The 340 held about 180 knots ground speed.

pages.tpl:
8 of 8
Lessons

What it teaches

  1. 1Announce your intentions and keep scanning outside. Here both pilots made proper calls and still collided.
  2. 2A pilot flying straight in should fit into the traffic already circling the airport.
  3. 3Pilots in the pattern should watch for straight in traffic, most of all on base before turning final.
